ImageContent.Description: Seen from above, the Kasilof River winds like a ribbon of turquoise through Alaska's Kenai Peninsula. The vivid blue water comes from glacial silt carried downstream from Tustumena Lake, one of the largest freshwater lakes in the state. Flowing about 27 kilometres before emptying into Cook Inlet, the river is shorter than its famous neighbour, the Kenai, but no less remarkable.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: The blue, glacier-fed waters of the Kasilof River, Alaska, United States

ImageContent.Description: Most first-time visitors know Jaipur, in Rajasthan, India, as the Pink City, but the earlier royal capital was centred on Amber Fort. That's where much of the dynasty's political and architectural history was shaped. The fort developed over more than a century, beginning under Raja Man Singh I in 1592 and continuing under later Kachwaha rulers who controlled the kingdom that eventually became Jaipur State. The royal family moved to the newly planned city of Jaipur in 1727, but Amber continued to serve ceremonial functions.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Sattais Katcheri Hall in Amber Fort near Jaipur, Rajasthan, India

ImageContent.Description: Forget rolling vineyards—around Stuttgart in Germany, the vines take the uphill route, climbing steep terraces above the Neckar valley and weaving between dry-stone walls. These vineyards are a defining feature of the city's landscape, with some of the steepest plots requiring extensive handwork because machinery is difficult to use. Local winegrowers, known as Wengerter, tend the vines on slopes that can reach gradients of 50 per cent. Traditional varieties such as Trollinger and Riesling are closely associated with the region and remain widely grown today.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Sunset over the vineyards of Steinhaldenfeld, Neckar valley, Stuttgart, Germany

ImageContent.Description: What do a bear's ears, a house on fire and a road packed with hairpin turns have in common? They're all part of the story of America's public lands in southeastern Utah. Bears Ears National Monument protects important cultural and natural resources, including archaeological sites that reflect thousands of years of human history. Its name comes from two buttes that rise side by side and resemble a bear's ears.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Cedar Mesa and Muley Point near Bears Ears National Monument, Utah, United States

ImageContent.Description: Most rivers spend their lives flowing around obstacles. The Sharavathi River reaches the edge of a cliff and simply jumps. At Jog Falls in Karnataka, the river plunges 253 metres, making it the third-highest waterfall in India.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Jog Falls, Sharavathi River, Karnataka, India

ImageContent.Description: Castelmezzano, in the province of Potenza in Basilicata, Italy, is hidden from view until you reach it. You arrive through a tunnel and as you emerge, the village suddenly appears, wedged among the sandstone pinnacles of the Lucanian Dolomites. The houses seem to climb over one another at around 750 metres above sea level, connected by steps and narrow lanes that rise towards the remains of the Norman fortress.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Castelmezzano, Basilicata, Italy

ImageContent.Description: A round door, a bright green frame and a hillside that looks straight out of Middle-earth—welcome to Hobbiton Movie Set in Matamata, New Zealand. Built in 1999 for 'The Lord of the Rings,' the original set featured 39 temporary Hobbit Holes across a 4.9-hectare site. After filming ended, the set was dismantled, but it returned in 2009 for 'The Hobbit' films and was rebuilt as a permanent attraction.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Hobbit house at Hobbiton Movie Set, Matamata, New Zealand

ImageContent.Description: What if a mountain range could show you its geological history in stripes? At Zhangye National Geopark in China, the rocks do exactly that. Designated as a UNESCO Global Geopark in 2020, Zhangye is in Gansu, a region linked to the ancient Silk Road. Here, ridges roll across the landscape in bands of red, orange, yellow, brown and other earthy tones. Known as the Danxia landform, this striking landscape was shaped by layers of sedimentary rock deposited over geological time. Tectonic forces later lifted and folded these layers, while weathering and erosion carved them into ridges, cliffs, gullies and peaks.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Danxia landform, Zhangye National Geopark, Gansu, China

ImageContent.Description: What can a 70-centimetre-tall bird teach us about life? Quite a lot. The Adélie penguin offers a lesson plan packed with resourcefulness, resilience and a little mischief. Found along the Antarctic coast, the species was named after Adèle, the wife of French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville, during the expedition that encountered the penguins in 1840.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Adélie penguins, Antarctica

ImageContent.Description: Castles usually come with towers, walls and at least one dramatic story. Château de Castelnaud in France has plenty of all three, plus medieval weapons. Rising around 150 metres above the Dordogne Valley, this 13th-century fortress commands views towards Château de Beynac and Périgord Noir. Its story is anything but quiet. During the Hundred Years' War, Castelnaud changed allegiance several times before French forces captured it after a three-week siege in 1442. Centuries later, the neglected fortress was used as a stone quarry before restoration began in 1965.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Château de Castelnaud overlooking the river Dordogne, France

ImageContent.Description: The season of big meals, bigger bellies and stocking up for winter is here. In Alaska, brown bears at Lake Clark National Park and Preserve make the most of the food still available in October. They feed on fish, sedges, berries, roots, clams and other foods to build up fat reserves. Some can weigh more than 450 kilograms before entering their dens for hibernation. That stored fat helps them survive the winter, when they do not eat or drink.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Brown bear in Silver Salmon Creek, Lake Clark National Park and Preserve, Alaska, United States

ImageContent.Description: Rivers have long played an important role in life across the world, supporting communities, wildlife and industry. Featured in today's image, the Chattooga River runs for about 92 kilometres across Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina in the United States. Flowing through the Appalachian Mountains, it winds between steep, forested slopes, rocky gorges and cascading rapids before reaching Lake Tugaloo. The river remains one of the Southeast's few major free-flowing rivers and is known for its scenery, whitewater recreation and wildlife.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Chattooga River in the Appalachian Mountains, North Carolina, United States

ImageContent.Description: In 1890, Yosemite became America's third national park. More than a century later, it still feels like a place that operates on geological time rather than human schedules. From Olmsted Point, the overlook in today's image, that timescale is impossible to miss. The smooth granite underfoot was sculpted by glaciers, while scattered boulders known as glacial erratics were carried here by ice and abandoned when it melted.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Sunset from Olmsted Point, Yosemite National Park, California, United States

ImageContent.Description: Balanced on a slender stalk in Norfolk, England, the male bearded reedling in today's image stands out with a pale blue-grey head, a bright orange bill and the black facial markings that give the species its name. Despite its striking appearance, this small bird spends much of its life hidden among the dense wetland vegetation of marshes, lakeshores and reed beds.
ImageContent.Headline: Info
ImageContent.Title: Male bearded reedling, Norfolk, England
